name: update-method
intent: Give every live object one self-contained per-frame step and let a single driver call each object's step every frame, so behaviour advances one frame at a time while input and rendering stay responsive.
problem: A running world is full of objects that each have to keep doing their own thing - guards patrolling, statues charging, agents acting - and the recurring decision is where one object's per-frame behaviour lives and how all those behaviours get driven. Coding a behaviour as a loop that runs to completion blocks input and rendering (the skeleton walks, but nobody sees it); coding it inline in the game loop turns the loop into a switchboard over every kind of object, so every new behaviour edits central code; and there is no way for two actors to evolve independently and simultaneously.
context: Real-time software with many concurrent live objects whose behaviour is mostly independent and must be simulated over time: games, agent-based simulations, animation and particle systems, tick-based servers and live visualisations. It is the natural partner of a frame driver (Game Loop) - the loop supplies the cadence, Update Method supplies the per-object step - and it becomes the wrong shape in turn-based or purely event-driven domains where nothing changes between inputs.
benefits: Each object's behaviour is one self-contained step that mutates only its own state, so objects stop knowing about each other and a new kind of actor is a new class/struct rather than an edit to a central switch.

Long-running behaviour becomes resumable: what used to be implicit in the program counter (which loop was running) turns into explicit object state, so a patrol or attack can suspend after one frame and continue on the next.

The single driver is a seam: it can walk only active objects, impose an order (tick groups, priorities, prerequisites), throttle or time-slice them, or partition them across threads without touching any per-object step.

Objects can appear and disappear at runtime without the driver knowing their concrete types, and the step can live on a component or a delegated state/type object instead of the entity class, so behaviour can be recomposed at runtime.
The order is explicit and repeatable, which is what replays, lockstep networking and step-by-step simulation tests need: each frame is a complete, self-consistent turn over the collection.
Steps are unit-testable in isolation: an object can be advanced by calling its update step directly with an explicit dt, without running the whole loop.
tradeoffs: Slicing behaviour into one-frame steps has a real up-front complexity cost: control flow must be re-expressed as stored state (which is why a state machine - the State pattern - is the pattern's frequent companion), and the code gets longer and more indirect than the straight-line version.

The objects are not truly concurrent: the walk is turn-based with one-frame turns, so update order is semantically significant - an object updated early acts on the previous frame's world while a later one already sees the new state. Double Buffer is the fix when every object must see a consistent snapshot; the sequential order is simultaneously the reason replays and lockstep networking are deterministic.

Modifying the collection during the walk is the classic failure mode: objects spawned mid-walk can act in the frame that created them, and removing an object shifts later elements, so the next one is silently skipped.

A per-frame virtual dispatch over a pointer-chasing collection costs one indirect call per object per frame and destroys locality; at large object counts the walk itself becomes the bottleneck (Data Locality/ECS are the answers), and dormant objects still pay for the walk unless a separate live-object collection is maintained and kept in sync.

Where the step lives is a design decision with migration cost: on the entity class it is simplest but brittle once kinds multiply, on components it decouples the parts of one entity, on a delegated State/Type Object it allows runtime behaviour swaps at the price of one more forwarding indirection.

Frame-sliced behaviour has no notion of scheduled future work and no protection against cross-object effects: an object that must act 'in three seconds' carries its own timer or needs a scheduler, and one step can still reach into another object's state in the same frame, which no ordering discipline prevents by itself.

participants.responsibility: Owns one slice of behaviour and the state needed to resume it; its update step advances exactly that state by one frame's worth of time and touches nothing else.

The single polymorphic hook the driver calls - a virtual/interface/trait method, a function pointer, or a suspension point - taking the frame's dt (or reading the engine's frame time) and returning without blocking.
Holds the live objects in a defined order and is the thing the driver walks; may be a master list with an active-only index, so dormant objects cost nothing.

Calls the update step on every object in the collection once per frame, owns the order (and, where supported, the threading), and never advances the world itself; in framework-hosted code this role is filled by the engine's tick registry or component system.
Supplies the elapsed time - the variable frame delta or the fixed step of Game Loop - to each update call; per-object steps never read the clock themselves.
Defers additions and removals until after the walk (dead flags, command buffers, deferred spawns) so the collection is not mutated while it is being iterated.

use_cases: Real-time games and simulations with many concurrent actors: patrolling guards, projectiles, particle effects and crowd agents each advance themselves once per frame while the driver walks the collection.

Component-based engines where the parts of one entity evolve independently - rendering, physics and AI components each implement their own step and the engine's registry dispatches per component (Unity, MonoGame, Bevy, GameplayKit, libGDX).
Per-frame animation and effect timelines outside games: tween/spring systems, sprite animation and UI transitions advanced from the browser's frame callback or a UI toolkit's animation timer.
Tick-based servers and headless simulations: game servers, digital twins and agent-based models where each agent's behaviour is a resumable step and the world advances in whole discrete frames.
Tools, editors and dashboards with continuously animating scenes, where many independent scene items (markers, live charts, gizmos) must advance on every repaint without a central per-item switch.

Porting straight-line behaviour into a frame loop: turning a scripted sequence (walk left, walk right) into a per-frame step, either by storing explicit state or by using coroutines/generators to keep the code linear.

Godot's SceneTree is the driver: a node opts into the walk with set_process(true) and its _process(delta) runs every render frame with the frame time passed in as an argument, while _physics_process(delta) is called at a fixed rate - so one object can implement two steps on two clocks and can leave the walk entirely (set_process(false)) instead of paying an enabled-flag check every frame.

Engines whose built-in driver leaves per-object order unspecified expose the order as configuration: Unity states you should not rely on the order of Update across GameObjects, so real projects fix dependencies through the Script Execution Order panel, a LateUpdate pass that runs after every Update, or the PlayerLoop API rather than through registration order.

Agent-based simulation models step whole populations in NetLogo: the go procedure runs ask turtles [ ... ] to give every agent its one turn and then tick advances the discrete clock - with documented semantics that agents take their turns in random order and only agents present when the ask began get to act.
avoid_when: Turn-based or purely event-driven domains where nothing changes between inputs (a chess board, a form-based tool): pieces do not need to update themselves, and the platform's event loop is the only loop you need.

The framework already dispatches per-object updates (Unity MonoBehaviour.Update, MonoGame GameComponent.Update, pygame Group.update, SpriteKit/GameplayKit, libGDX Stage.act, Bevy systems): implement the callback and register, do not build a second dispatch layer on top.
The objects are passive data and one system owns the logic: a data-oriented pass over a flat array (or a single switch over a tag) is faster and simpler than a virtual call per object.

Object counts are large and the per-frame dispatch dominates (tens of thousands of particles): batch the behaviour - a particle system, SoA layout, or ECS - instead of paying one indirect call and one pointer chase per object.

The behaviour must see a consistent snapshot of the whole world every frame (simultaneous semantics): use Double Buffer so every object reads the previous frame, or make the order provably irrelevant.

The behaviour is a long-lived control flow with its own blocking logic (scripted sequences, cutscenes): explicit state machines or coroutines/fibers express it without forcing every branch into an update body.
anti_patterns: God update: one update body that handles AI, physics, input and presentation for an entity, dissolving the single responsibility the pattern depends on and turning each frame into a switchboard.

Virtual update on everything, including inert objects (resting projectiles, off-screen entities), so the collection is walked and dispatched for objects that do nothing - the enabled-flag check is the symptom.
Unmanaged mutation during the walk: spawning, killing or reordering objects inside update with no deferred phase, producing skipped objects, double-steps and heisenbugs.
Undocumented order dependence: behaviour that only works because one object happens to be registered before another, with the implicit sequencing treated as an implementation detail.

Rebuilding framework dispatch: a hand-written component/entity system layered beside the engine's own (Unity Update, Bevy systems, pygame Group.update), so both walk the objects and neither owns the semantics.
Threading the walk blindly: stepping objects on several threads while steps reach into shared world state, buying data races instead of parallelism.
design_principles: Single responsibility: one object, one per-frame step - the pattern is only as good as the smallness of that step.
Polymorphism over type switching: the driver dispatches through an abstract hook, so new kinds of object never edit the driver (open/closed).
Explicit state over implicit control flow: anything needed to resume next frame is part of the object's state, not of a blocked call stack (encapsulation).
Inversion of control: the driver calls your step; objects do not own the cadence and must not block or render.
Separation of the walk from the world's semantics: the driver guarantees order and lifetime, while each step guarantees it advances only its own state by exactly one dt.
best_practices: Pass dt into the step explicitly and never let it read the clock; this keeps steps testable, replayable and independent of the frame rate.
Define and document the update order (tick groups, prerequisite edges, registration order) and express real dependencies explicitly instead of relying on the order objects were created.
Never mutate the collection while walking it: keep a dead flag and compact afterwards, cache the iteration count at loop entry, or buffer spawns and despawns until the walk is done.
Keep a separate collection or index of active objects when many are dormant, rather than checking an enabled flag on every object every frame.

Keep steps small and single-purpose; move multi-state behaviour into a state machine or a delegated type/state object, and resolve cross-object effects in a later phase or system instead of inside individual steps.
Make every step a pure function of (own state, dt, inputs): no cross-object writes, no allocation spikes, no blocking calls, no rendering.
Bound the per-frame work (throttle or stagger expensive steps across frames) so a single object cannot blow the frame budget for everyone.
Profile the walk as object counts grow: when dispatch and cache misses dominate, move the behaviour to systems over flat arrays (Data Locality/ECS) instead of micro-optimising the virtual call.
sources: Nystrom (2014), Game Programming Patterns, 'Sequencing Patterns: Update Method' - the originating catalogue entry: intent ('Simulate a collection of independent objects by telling each to process one frame of behavior at a time'), the pattern statement (the game world maintains a collection of objects; each implements an update method that simulates one frame; each frame the game updates every object in the collection), when to use it (independent objects simulated over time; a poor fit for chess-like pieces), the 'Keep in Mind' sections (explicit resume state, the significance of update order, careless list modification) and the design decisions (update on the entity class vs component vs delegated state/type object; dormant-object handling). https://gameprogrammingpatterns.com/update-method.html

Unity Scripting API, MonoBehaviour.Update() - 'Update is called every frame, if the MonoBehaviour is enabled'; Time.deltaTime is the elapsed time since the last call, and the engine walks every enabled component. https://docs.unity3d.com/ScriptReference/MonoBehaviour.Update.html

Apple Developer Documentation, SpriteKit SKScene update(_:) - 'Do not call this method directly; it is called by the system exactly once per frame, so long as the scene is presented in a view and is not paused'; the primary place for in-game simulation logic. https://developer.apple.com/documentation/spritekit/skscene/update(_:)

pygame documentation, pygame.sprite - Sprite.update is 'a convenient hook that you can override', and Group.update 'Calls the update() method on all Sprites in the Group', passing the same arguments to every sprite. https://www.pygame.org/docs/ref/sprite.html

Bevy documentation, bevy_app::Update - 'The schedule that contains any app logic that must run once per render frame', with FixedUpdate for fixed-rate gameplay logic; the modern data-oriented realization where per-frame steps are systems over queries. https://docs.rs/bevy/latest/bevy/app/struct.Update.html

MDN Web Docs, Window.requestAnimationFrame() - 'requests the browser to call a user-supplied callback function before the next repaint', passes the timestamp of the previous frame's rendering end, and is paused in background tabs. https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Window/requestAnimationFrame

Godot Engine documentation, Node._process() and Node._physics_process() - normal processing is toggled with set_process() and 'happens as fast as possible and is dependent on the frame rate, so the processing time delta (in seconds) is passed as an argument', while physics processing 'happens a fixed number of times per second (60 by default)'; process_priority and process_mode govern order and pausing per node. https://docs.godotengine.org/en/stable/classes/class_node.html

Unity Manual, Order of execution for event functions - 'you should not rely on the order in which the same event function is invoked for different GameObjects - except when the order is explicitly documented or settable'; the Script Execution Order panel, the after-everything LateUpdate phase and the PlayerLoop API are the engine's order-control seams. https://docs.unity3d.com/2022.3/Documentation/Manual/ExecutionOrder.html

NetLogo Dictionary, ask - the per-tick driver step for agent-based models: 'when ask is used with an agentset each agent will take its turn in a random order' and 'Only the agents that are in the agentset at the time the ask begins run the commands'; the companion tick command advances the discrete model clock one whole turn at a time. https://docs.netlogo.org/dict/ask.html

Data-Oriented Design book (online release), 'What's wrong?' - the canonical criticism of the per-object virtual update walk: calling update() through a vtable across an array of heterogeneous objects loads the vtable pointer per object, evicts instruction and data cache and dirties branch-predictor slots, so the cost is real but 'spread thinly over the whole of the processing' and rarely shows up in profiles - the argument for replacing the walk with systems over flat data at scale. https://dataorienteddesign.com/dodbook/node12.html
